# Part 1: Importing data with R packages

## 1.1 - Female labour force participation (ILO)

**1.1.1 - Explain which indicator you’ve chosen, and describe it briefly in words.**

The ILOSTAT table of contents lists every series whose name contains "Labour force participation". 
The same rate is published in many versions, broken down by different characteristics.

```{r}

# Download the ILOSTAT table of contents for "Labour force participation"

toc <- get_ilostat_toc(search = "Labour force participation",quiet  = TRUE)
toc

# explore the number of indicator present in toc (characteristic of the different dataset contained in ILO)

dim(toc)
names(toc)
```

```{r}
# Identification of the different dataset

toc%>%as.data.frame()%>%select(id, freq, data.start, data.end, n.ref_area, indicator, n.records)%>%arrange(data.start)%>%print()

```

Our research question is about long-run structural change, so we need annual data. 
Monthly and quarterly series cover fewer countries and would add seasonality we don't need.

```{r}

annual <- toc %>%as.data.frame() %>%filter(freq == "A")                         # "A" = annual
annual

# number of candidates remaining
nrow(annual)                       
```

To keep women aged 45 to 54, the series must be split by both sex and age. 
Series split by sex and another characteristic (education, rural/urban area, marital status) but not by age cannot be used.

```{r}
candidate <- annual %>%
  filter(startsWith(id, "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE")) %>%                                # broken down by sex AND age
  select(id, indicator.label, data.start, data.end, n.ref_area, n.records) %>%
  arrange(data.start)                                                           # oldest start year first
candidate
```

```{r}
# Which candidate covers the most countries and regions?
candidate %>%select(id, n.ref_area)%>%arrange(desc(n.ref_area))%>%print()    # desc() = largest first
```
Seven annual series give the labour force participation rate broken down by both sex and age. Only EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A (“Labour force participation rate by sex and age (%)”) starts in 1946, which makes it the only series covering the whole period from 1950 that our research question needs.

Thus we decided to choose the indicator: EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A, "Labour force participation rate by sex and age (%)", annual data.

It measures the share of the working-age population in a given sex and age group that is economically active (employed or looking for an employment). We are then able to select the share of women bewteen 45 and 54 that are economically active.

We have chosen this indicator because :

- It has the longest time series and the most countries.
- It can easily filter for the women in the right age bracket.
- The frequency "annual" matches best the research question (long-run structural pattern: how female participation changes as countries develop). The extra detail of monthly or quarterly data would not be particularly relevant. We will not need to deal with seasonality. Higher frequency series are only available for limited amount of countries as it requires frequent surveys which cost money. For our research question, we need a sample that includes countries at different income level.
- For the rest of the project, it will allow us to merge it with GDP as the frequency is also annual. 

**1.1.2 - Import the full series, i.e. all years available from 1950 to 2025. **

We now download the series chosen in 1.1.1. 
Since we only need women aged 45 to 54, we use the filters of `get_ilostat()`, so the ILO server sends only the rows we need instead of the full dataset.

To filter by age, we need the exact code ILOSTAT uses for the 45 to 54 age group. We first check which age codes exist, using a small download (Swiss women only) as an example.

```{r}
test <- get_ilostat(
  id      = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",     # our chosen dataset
  segment = "indicator",                 # the dataset is organised by indicator
  filters = list(ref_area = "CHE",       # only Switzerland, to keep it small
                 sex      = "SEX_F"),    # only women
  quiet   = TRUE
)

test %>% distinct(classif1) %>% filter(startsWith(classif1, "AGE_10YRBANDS"))   # show only the 10-year bands

```

The ILO publishes the same data in several age-grouping systems (youth/adult, broad aggregates, 10-year and 5-year bands). The 10-year bands include the group we need, with the code `AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54`.

We can now download the full series for all countries, keeping only women aged 45 to 54 and the years 1950 to 2025.

```{r}
# Download the full series: all countries, women aged 45-54, 1950-2025
flfp_raw <- get_ilostat(
  id          = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",
  segment     = "indicator",
  time_format = "num",                    # years as numbers, not text
  filters     = list(
    sex      = "SEX_F",                   # women
    classif1 = "AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54",    # age group 45-54 (code checked above)
    timefrom = 1950,                      # first year
    timeto   = 2025                       # last year
  ),
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Checks
distinct(flfp_raw, sex, classif1)  # should be one row: SEX_F, AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54
range(flfp_raw$year)                   # first and last year
n_distinct(flfp_raw$iso3)              # number of countries and regions

```

# 1.2 - GDP per capita (World Bank)

## 1.2.1 - Explain which indicator you’ve chosen, and describe it briefly in words.

We will use lthe [WDI package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/WDI/index.html)

We search for the indicators whose name contains "GDP per capita"

```{r}
search_wdi <- WDIsearch(string = "GDP per capita", field = "name") %>%as.data.frame()
```

We filter for criteria (1) and (2), which are read from the indicator name:
- same currency: "US`$`" or "international `$`" (not "LCU" = local currency)
- inflation-adjusted: "constant" prices, ) measure GDP every year at the prices of one base year (not "current")

```{r}
candidates_W <- search_wdi %>% mutate(
    same_currency = grepl("US\\$|international \\$", name),
    inflation_adj = grepl("constant", name, ignore.case = TRUE)
  )

candidates_W
```

Finally, we filter for criterion 3: we download the already filtered candidates and compare their coverage.
We compare how far back each one goes and how many countries it covers:

```{r}

# Criteria (1) and (2): keep indicators with TRUE in both columns

finalists <- candidates_W %>% filter(same_currency, inflation_adj)

df_finalists <- WDI(
  country   = "all",
  indicator = finalists$indicator,
  # start     = 1960, note that the start date could be added however the data collection always start in 1960
  end       = 2025,
  extra     = TRUE   # adds "region", used to drop aggregates like "World"
)

# Now adding the last constraint (3) : it compares how far back and how widely each finalist is covered
coverage <- df_finalists %>%
  filter(region != "Aggregates") %>%   # keep countries only
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = any_of(finalists$indicator),
    names_to  = "indicator",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
  group_by(indicator) %>%
  summarise(
    first_year  = min(year),             # earliest year with data
    last_year   = max(year),             # latest year with data
    n_countries = n_distinct(iso3c),     # how many countries
    n_obs       = n()                    # number of country-year values
  ) %>%
  arrange(first_year)

coverage
```

To conclude, we will keep NY.GDP.PCAP.KD as it starts the furthest back in time (1960) and covers the most countries. (213>199)

It is the total value of goods and services produced in the country's economy, divided by its midyear population. The values are in US dollars, and the base year is 2015 (adjusted for inflation).

## 1.2.2 - Import the full series, i.e. all years available up to 2025. What is the oldest date available? 

Now that we have selected the indicator, we import the entier series from the earliest date possible. In our case, we know from before that the series starts in 1960.

```{r}
# Import GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) for all countries, all years up to 2025
df_wb <- WDI(
  country   = "all",
  indicator = c(gdp_pc = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD"),
  start     = 1960,
  end       = 2025
)

df_wb
```

```{r}
# Oldest year with data
min(df_wb$year[!is.na(df_wb$gdp_pc)])
```

We have here the confirmation that the earliest date available is 1960.

# Part 2: Programming your own API functions


```{r}

#Work done for now

# Load our own API functions from the R/ folder
source("api_ILO.R")  # creates get_ilodata()
source("api_WB.R")   # creates get_wbdata()

# 2. Quick test: does each function work for one country? --------------------
get_ilodata("CHE", year_from = 2020, year_to = 2023)
get_wbdata("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", "CHE", year_from = 2020, year_to = 2023)


# 3. Test for Switzerland, USA and Germany in 2023 ----------------------------

countries <- c("CHE", "USA", "DEU")

# ILO: female labour force participation rate, women aged 45-54
ilo_test <- lapply(countries, get_ilodata, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023) |>
  bind_rows()
ilo_test

# World Bank: GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)
wb_test <- lapply(
  countries,
  function(cty) get_wbdata("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", cty, 2023, 2023)
) |>
  bind_rows()
wb_test


# 4. Full download: all countries, all years ----------------------------------

ilo_all <- get_ilodata()  # all countries, 1950-2025
wb_all <- get_wbdata()    # all countries, 1960-2025

nrow(ilo_all)  # the ILO explorer showed 4130 data points for these filters
nrow(wb_all)
```

## Female labour force participation (ILO)

### Retrieve data using your own API wrapper

[Your 2-3 sentences: how the URL is built. Base URL + dataflow (agency, dataset ID, version) + key (one slot per dimension, separated by dots, empty slot = all values) + query parameters (start year, end year, format).]

```{r, file = "R/get_ilodata.R"}
```

### Test your API

**1.** [Your comment on the output of your own function.]

```{r}
# Countries to test (ISO 3-letter codes used by the ILO)
countries <- c("CHE", "USA", "DEU")

# Own function, applied to each country with lapply(), then stacked
df_own <- lapply(countries, get_ilodata, year_from = 2023, year_to = 2023) |>
  bind_rows()

# Keep the columns we need to compare
df_own_short <- df_own |>
  select(ref_area = REF_AREA, time = TIME_PERIOD, value_api = OBS_VALUE)

df_own_short
```

**2.** [Your answer: are the results the same as with Rilostat?]

```{r}
# Same request with the Rilostat package
df_pkg <- get_ilostat(
  id = "EAP_DWAP_SEX_AGE_RT_A",
  time_format = "num",
  filters = list(
    ref_area = countries,
    sex = "SEX_F",
    classif1 = "AGE_10YRBANDS_Y45-54",
    timefrom = 2023,
    timeto = 2023
  )
)

# Put both results side by side and compute the difference
comparison <- df_pkg |>
  select(ref_area, time, value_pkg = obs_value) |>
  inner_join(df_own_short, by = c("ref_area", "time")) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

comparison
```

[Your answer: are the results the same as with WDI?]

```{r}
# Own function, applied to each country with lapply(), then stacked
countries_wb <- c("CHE", "USA", "DEU")

df_wb_own <- lapply(
  countries_wb,
  function(cty) get_wbdata("NY.GDP.PCAP.KD", cty, 2023, 2023)
) |>
  bind_rows()

df_wb_own

# Same request with the WDI package
df_wb_pkg <- WDI(
  country = c("CH", "US", "DE"),
  indicator = "NY.GDP.PCAP.KD",
  start = 2023,
  end = 2023
)

# Put both results side by side and compute the difference
comparison_wb <- df_wb_pkg |>
  select(iso3c, year, value_pkg = NY.GDP.PCAP.KD) |>
  inner_join(
    df_wb_own |> select(iso3c, year, value_api = value),
    by = c("iso3c", "year")
  ) |>
  mutate(difference = value_api - value_pkg)

comparison_wb
```
